upheaval.inYou: If you have wept through a long night, hear the promise that does not pretend you have not been crying: the night ends. Joy comes in the morning. Your tears were never pointless leaking; they were seed sown in dark ground, and such seed has a harvest by promise. You may not see the dawn yet. But it is the nature of nights to end. Keep the last watch.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that has wept through a long night can forget the night is a night at all. It needs to hear that its grief is a lodger and not the owner, that the tears a community sowed in its wilderness were seed and not waste. The dawn the body cannot yet see is, by the shape of the promise, already on its way.
upheaval.whatRemains: Hebrews says what can be shaken is shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain. The night is among the things that pass; by definition it is the part of the story that gets removed. What remains beneath it is the unshakable certainty of morning — the God whose mercies are new every dawn.
reflection: What has my long night been telling me that it is permanent, when it is only a night?
Can I believe the tears I have sown were seed and not waste, even with no harvest in sight?
What would it look like for me to keep the last watch as one who knows morning is coming?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, my night has felt less like weather and more like the world. Teach me to call it a night again, with a morning fastened to its end. Let the tears I have sown be seed in Your dark ground. Keep me through the last watch until the joy You promised comes. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 30:5 (joy comes in the morning); Psalm 126:5 (sow in tears, reap in joy).

title: The dawn from on high
moment:
Old Zechariah had been silent for nine months, struck wordless at the altar for doubting a promise. When his tongue is finally loosed, the first thing it does is sing — and the song is not chiefly about his own son. It reaches past John to the dawn coming behind him: because of the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will visit those who sit in darkness. Notice where the dawn comes from. Not up from the horizon of human effort, not kindled by people straining to make their own light. It comes from on high. It is a visitation.

Peter says the same thing from the other side. Hold to the word, he writes, like a lamp shining in a dark place — until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. The lamp is what you tend while it is still night. But the lamp is not the dawn, and you cannot promote it into one by trying harder. The day breaks of its own accord. The morning star rises when it rises. The turn out of the long disorientation arrives, in the end, as a gift let down from above, not a glow worked up from below.
voiceQuote: Because of the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will visit us.
scriptureText: You do well to take heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the morning star arises in your hearts.
weight:
There is a particular exhaustion that comes from trying to manufacture your own dawn. You have done the work. You have read the books, prayed the prayers, tried to feel again, lain in the dark willing the light to come — and it will not come on command, and the failure to summon it becomes one more proof that the dark is winning. Zechariah's song lifts that whole weight off you. You were never meant to generate the dawn. It comes from on high, mercy visiting people sitting exactly where you are, in the dark.

This does not leave you with nothing to do; it tells you what your actual work is. Not to make the morning, but to keep the lamp lit through the last of the night. To hold to the word when it gives no warmth, the way you would tend a small flame in a long power outage — not because the flame is the sunrise, but because it keeps you until the sunrise. And the dawn does its own rising. The morning star comes up in hearts that had given up trying to light themselves.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn, and the turn names its own source. The light at the end of the wilderness is not a thing the wanderer produces by effort or insight; it breaks in from above as a visitation of mercy. The phase asks you to stop straining to make your own morning and to keep faithful with the lamp until the day breaks on its own.
upheaval.inYou: You cannot manufacture your own dawn, and the good news is that you were never asked to. The dayspring comes from on high, a visitation of tender mercy to people sitting exactly where you sit, in the dark. Your task in the last of the night is small: tend the lamp of His word until the day breaks of itself and the morning star rises in a heart too tired to light itself.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church cannot engineer its own renewal, however many programs it runs at the problem. The dawn comes from on high. A community's work in the dark is humbler: to keep tending the lamp of the word and to wait for the visitation of mercy that breaks in on its own timing. The renewal a body longs for is finally a gift that arrives, not an outcome it executes.
upheaval.whatRemains: What can be shaken includes every light we kindle for ourselves; our manufactured dawns gutter and go out. What cannot be shaken is the tender mercy of God, the dayspring that visits from on high. When all the lamps we lit by our own effort have failed, the dawn He sends remains, rising over those who only sat and waited.
reflection: Where have I worn myself out trying to manufacture a dawn I was only ever meant to wait for?
What would it look like for me, today, to tend the lamp of the word without mistaking it for the sunrise?
Can I trust that the dayspring comes from on high, on God's timing rather than mine?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I am tired from trying to light my own morning, and the dark only deepened. Let me lay that work down and tend the lamp of Your word through the last of the night. Send Your dawn from on high; let Your morning star rise in a heart too weary to rise on its own. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 1:78 (the dawn from on high will visit us); 2 Peter 1:19 (until the day dawns and the morning star rises).

title: A shoot from the stump
moment:
By Isaiah's day the royal line of David had been cut down to a stump. The proud tree of the house of Jesse was lopped off at the root, the kingdom felled, only a low stub of dead wood left where a dynasty had stood. Anyone walking past would have read it as finished — that is what a stump is, the visible end of a tree. But Isaiah, looking at the same severed wood, sees what the casual eye would miss: a shoot coming forth out of the stump of Jesse, a branch out of those old roots that would bear fruit. Not a new tree planted at a safe distance from the failure, but a green shoot pushing up out of the very roots everyone had written off.

Job had seen the principle long before, in any felled tree: there is hope for a cut-down tree to sprout again, its tender branch not ceasing. There is a stubborn life in roots the axe does not reach. This is the signature of the long disorientation beginning to turn — not renewal imported from somewhere undamaged, but new life rising out of the exact place that looked dead. God has a way of coming up green out of grey stumps.
voiceQuote: There shall come forth a shoot out of the stump of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots shall bear fruit.
scriptureText: There is hope for a tree, if it is cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its tender branch will not cease.
weight:
There is a stump somewhere in your life, and you have stopped looking at it because looking hurts. The calling that got cut off at the root. The relationship lopped down to dead wood. The faith that once stood like a tree and is now a stub you walk past quickly, ashamed of how much you once expected from it. You have filed it under finished, because that is what a stump means. The tree is over. Make your peace.

Isaiah's vision is an argument against that filing. God specializes, of all things, in the green shoot out of exactly such stumps. The part you can see is not the whole story; the roots are still in the ground, and a tender branch can come up from roots the axe never reached. What looks finished above the surface may be alive below it. This is not a promise that the old tree returns as it was — the shoot is new growth, not the felled trunk restored. But it refuses to let you call the stump dead just because it is cut down.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn, seen in the lowest place — new life rising from what looked cut down and dead. The phase asks you not to confirm the verdict your eyes have already passed on the stump. The wilderness is not yet over, and the shoot is still tender and small, but life is stirring in roots you thought the axe had finished.
upheaval.inYou: Look at the stump you have stopped looking at — the calling, the bond, the faith that got cut to dead wood. Isaiah's vision is that God grows green shoots out of precisely such stumps. What looks finished above the ground may be alive below it. The tender branch may already be pushing up from roots you grieved as dead. Do not pass the verdict the wood has not earned.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church cut down to a stump — its old life lopped off, only dead wood apparently left — is precisely the ground in which God grows a green shoot. The new branch rises not from somewhere fresh but from the old severed roots. A community should not write off its own stump. The shoot of renewal so often comes up from the very wood the body had buried.
upheaval.whatRemains: What can be shaken is the standing tree, the visible structure, the part the axe can reach; all of that comes down. What cannot be shaken runs deeper than the cut — the root of Jesse, the life God keeps in reserve below the surface. When the tree of every visible thing has fallen, that hidden root remains, still sending up green.
reflection: Which stump in my life have I quietly filed under finished, and stopped daring to look at?
Can I believe there is life in roots the axe never reached, even where the tree is clearly down?
What would change if I treated the cut-down place as ground for a shoot rather than a grave?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have written off the stump as dead and stopped expecting anything from it. You see roots the axe never reached. Send up Your green shoot from the very wood I grieved, in Your time and not on my command. Teach me to wait there as one who has heard there is still hope. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 11:1 (a shoot from the stump of Jesse); Job 14:7 (hope for a cut-down tree to sprout).

title: Do you not perceive it?
moment:
There is a gentle challenge folded into the middle of one of God's tenderest promises. Behold, He says through Isaiah, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth. And then, before the comfort can settle, the question: will you not perceive it? It is asked of people still sitting in the rubble of the old, still turned to face what they lost. The new thing is not in the distant future waiting to be announced with trumpets. It is springing forth already, now, while you are still grieving — and the danger is not that it will fail to come but that you will fail to see it.

For the new rarely arrives looking like the old. A way is opening in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, but a way through trackless country does not look like the road you knew, and water in sand is easy to miss when your eyes are full of the river you remember. Isaiah presses the same point again: God has been showing them new things, hidden things they had not known. Hidden things. Part of how the long disorientation begins to turn is the slow, deliberate work of learning to perceive the new thing God has quietly already started.
voiceQuote: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; will you not perceive it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
scriptureText: I have showed you new things from this time, even hidden things, which you have not known.
weight:
Grief has a way of fixing your eyes on what is gone. It is natural; it may even be right for a season. But it carries a cost the grieving rarely notice: while your face is turned back toward the old thing you lost, the new thing can be springing up right behind you, unseen. God's question is not a rebuke. It is tender, but pointed: will you not perceive it. He is asking you to turn your head.

Because the new thing almost never announces itself. It does not arrive looking like the old restored. It comes small — a door you would not have called a door, a relationship you did not expect, a quiet steadiness where there used to be a roar. If you wait for the new to look like the old come back, you will walk straight past the rivers breaking out in your own desert. So the discipline of the turn is partly a discipline of the eyes: to look forward as well as back, and to take seriously that God may already be doing the very thing you are still praying He would begin.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn, and the turn here is as much about seeing as about happening. The new thing may already be springing forth while the old grief still holds the eye. The phase asks you to train your sight forward — not to abandon the grieving, but to refuse to let it blind you to the rivers God is already opening in the desert.
upheaval.inYou: God may already be doing the new thing, springing it up small in the corners of your wilderness while your face is still turned to the old. His question is gentle but pointed: will you not perceive it. Train your eyes to notice the first green growth, the unlikely door, the way opening where you were sure there was none. The new is often well underway before we see it.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church grieving what it has lost can miss the new thing God is springing up in its midst, because the new so rarely resembles the old. The LORD's question presses a community to perceive: where are the rivers breaking out in your desert, the small growth you have been too sad to see? The turn toward new bearings begins with eyes that learn to see what God has already begun.
upheaval.whatRemains: What can be shaken is the old thing we keep facing — the form that is passing, the road that is gone. What cannot be shaken is the God who is always making, whose new thing springs forth even in the desert. When the old is removed, His creating remains, opening rivers in the very wilderness we thought was only loss.
reflection: Where has my grief for the old thing kept my eyes from turning to the new?
What small, unfamiliar growth might already be springing up that I have been too sad to perceive?
Am I waiting for the new thing to look like the old, and so missing the way God is actually opening?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, my face has been turned to what I lost, and I may have walked past the new thing You were already beginning. Forgive my unperceiving eyes. Open them to the rivers breaking out in my desert, the way opening where I saw none. Let me grieve without going blind to the new. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 43:19 (a new thing springing forth, a way in the wilderness); Isaiah 48:6 (new things, hidden things).

title: The desert shall blossom
moment:
When Isaiah sees the end of the wilderness, he does not see the people finally escaping it. He sees the wilderness itself change. The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad, and the desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose. The dry land is not abandoned for greener country; it is made glad. The desert does not stay a desert the people are at last led out of; it rejoices, it blossoms, it breaks into flower where there had been only sand. And the water that does it comes up in the unlikeliest place of all: in the wilderness itself, waters break out, streams run in the desert. Not somewhere beyond it, after the long crossing. In it.

This is a deeper hope than rescue, and it is worth sitting with the difference. Rescue gets you out of the hard place. What Isaiah sees is the hard place itself transformed — the very ground of your thirst becoming the ground of bloom. God does not only lead His people out of deserts. He has a way of making the desert flower, so that the soil of the worst season turns out, in time, to be the most fruitful of all.
voiceQuote: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
scriptureText: In the wilderness waters shall break out, and streams in the desert.
weight:
When you are in a long dry season, the only outcome you can imagine wanting is out. Get me out of this. Lead me somewhere else, anywhere that is not this barren stretch. That prayer is honest and God hears it. But Isaiah holds out something better than the exit you are praying for, and it is worth letting your hope grow large enough to take it in: not merely escape from the desert, but the blossoming of it. The very place that has been dry and barren becoming, in God's hands, the most fruitful ground you will ever stand on.

This reframes the whole season. If the desert can blossom, then the years in it are not a write-off to survive and forget. The thirst, the barrenness, the long ache for water — these may turn out to be the very conditions in which something grows that could grow nowhere else. Waters break out in the wilderness — in it, not after it. So do not pray so hard for the exit that you miss the bloom. God may not relocate you. He may make this dry place flower under your feet.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn, and the hope here runs deeper than rescue. The wilderness is not merely escaped; it is transformed — blossom where there was only sand. The phase asks you to widen your hope past the exit you keep praying for, and to believe that the very ground of your disorientation can become, in God's hands, the most fruitful place of all.
upheaval.inYou: The hope here is better than the exit you keep asking for: the desert of your disorientation can itself blossom. The ground that was dry and barren can become, in God's hands, the most fruitful soil of your life. Waters break out where you least expected them — in the wilderness, not after it. God may not lead you elsewhere; He may make this dry place bloom beneath your feet.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church longing only to escape its wilderness may miss the greater promise: the desert itself can blossom. The very season of dryness can become, in God's hands, the ground of unexpected fruitfulness, with streams breaking out where the community knew only thirst. The turn toward new bearings is sometimes not relocation but transformation — the very place the body suffered becoming the place it flowers.
upheaval.whatRemains: What can be shaken is the assumption that the dry place is only to be fled, that barren ground can do nothing but be left behind. What cannot be shaken is the God who makes deserts blossom and breaks streams out of sand. When every other ground has failed, His power to make the wilderness itself flower remains.
reflection: Have I prayed so single-mindedly for the exit that I cannot imagine the desert itself blooming?
What might be growing in the dry ground of my season that could grow nowhere else?
Can I trust God to make this place flower, even if He does not lead me out of it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have prayed for the way out of this desert and meant every word. Enlarge my hope to receive something better: the desert itself blossoming. Break Your streams out in this wilderness, not only beyond it. Make the dry ground of this season the most fruitful soil I have ever stood on. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 35:1, 6 (the desert blossoms; waters break out in the wilderness).

title: Up from the pit
moment: David has a word for the place where nothing holds. He calls it a horrible pit, and then, in case the picture were too clean, the miry clay — not a dry hole you could brace against and climb, but mud that takes whatever weight you put on it and gives nothing back. You cannot get a foothold in miry clay. Every push down is a sinking. This is the precise physics of the disoriented soul: the harder you work to climb out, the deeper you go. And then, into that helplessness, God acts. He reaches down and lifts. David does not say he found a ledge or summoned his strength; he says he was brought up, carried out of the slime by a hand not his own. Two things follow the rescue, and they answer the two miseries of the pit. The feet that found nothing to stand on are set on a rock, a firm place at last. And the mouth that could only cry from the mud is given a new song. The God who pulls people out of pits does not leave them merely dried off and shaking. He gives them ground, and He gives them a tune they did not have before.
voiceQuote: He brought me up out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay; he set my feet on a rock, and gave me a firm place to stand.
scriptureText: He has put a new song in my mouth, even praise to our God; many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
weight: The new song is the part we rush past, and the part that turns a private rescue into something larger. David does not say the song stays in his own mouth. He says many will see it and come to trust the LORD. The deliverance you cannot yet imagine has, folded inside it, a witness you cannot yet imagine either. This matters for the long middle, because in the pit you can sing nothing. The mud is in your throat. If anyone told you to praise from down there, you would rightly hate them for it. So hear the order David keeps: first the lifting, then the rock, then the song, never reversed. The song is not rent you pay to be rescued. It is the overflow of feet that have finally found something solid. You do not fail the turn by having no song tonight. The song belongs to the far side of the rescue, and the rescue is God's to give. When it comes, the firmness underfoot will loosen your tongue on its own, and the thing you despaired through becomes the reason another sinking soul looks up.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn — the pit not yet a memory, but the hand already reaching. The phase asks you to wait for a rescue you cannot perform, to stop clawing at miry clay long enough to be lifted. The turn is not your climb out. It is the moment a strength not your own sets your feet on rock.
upheaval.inYou: If you are in the miry clay, where nothing holds and every effort sinks you deeper, stop measuring the turn by whether you can climb. You cannot, and you were never meant to. The hand that lifts is not yours. Your part is to keep crying upward from the mud. The rock is coming, and after it, a song you do not have yet.
upheaval.inTheBody: A community sunk in the miry clay learns the same hard physics: programs and pushing only deepen the sinking. The body waits for the God who reaches into pits, not for its own ingenuity to find a ledge. And when He lifts it onto rock, the new song He gives is never kept indoors. A church rescued from the mud becomes a reason watching strangers begin to trust the LORD.
upheaval.whatRemains: When the mud takes every foothold, you learn what was never miry at all. The rock God sets you on cannot be shaken — not the ground you stood on before, which gave way, but the firm place beneath every footing. What is removed is the false ground; what remains is the One who is Himself the rock.
reflection: Where am I clawing at miry clay, trying to climb out of a pit only God can lift me from?
Have I been waiting to be lifted, or exhausting myself to be impressive in the mud?
If I have no new song yet, can I trust that it belongs to the far side of a rescue still coming?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I am in the miry clay, and every effort to climb has only taken me deeper. I cannot lift myself. Reach down. Set my feet on the rock that does not move, and in time put a new song in my mouth — one another sinking soul might hear, and trust You too. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 40:2-3 (up from the miry pit, feet on a rock, a new song).

title: Like those who dream
moment: Seventy years is long enough to forget that exile ends. A generation born in Babylon had never seen Zion; they knew the songs of home only as their parents' grief, the harps hung on the willows, the question of how to sing the LORD's song in a strange land. And then the impossible word arrives: you may go home. The psalm that remembers it does not reach first for triumph. It reaches for a stranger feeling — we were like those who dream. Not we rejoiced, not we marched out in glory, but we walked around dazed, unsure the ground was real, the way you move through the first minutes of waking when the good news has not yet been believed by the body. The mouth, the psalm says, filled with laughter; the tongue with singing. But underneath the laughter is the disbelief that makes the laughter what it is. The deliverance was too long-prayed and too far gone to trust on first sight. So they pinched themselves and laughed and could only say the plainest true thing there was to say: the LORD has done great things for us. The exile they had stopped expecting to end had ended.
voiceQuote: When the LORD brought back those who returned to Zion, we were like those who dream.
scriptureText: The LORD has done great things for us, and we are glad.
weight: There is a particular danger in a long disorientation, and it is not despair. Despair at least keeps the question alive. The deeper danger is that you quietly stop expecting the turn at all — you make a permanent home in Babylon, decorate the captivity, and call wanting more naive. The returning exiles had every reason to have done exactly that. Seventy years is a lifetime. And the grace of this psalm is that it does not scold them for the dazed disbelief; it honors it. The dreamlike quality is not weak faith. It is the honest response of people for whom the rescue is genuinely too large for the size their hope had shrunk to. So if God brings the reversal you had given up daring to name, you may not feel the clean joy you once imagined. You may feel unsteady, suspicious of your own happiness, half-waiting for it to dissolve. Let it be. Laughter and disbelief can share one mouth. The dream is real this time, and all the moment asks of you is the sentence the exiles found: the LORD has done great things.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn at its most communal — a whole people's wilderness actually ending. The phase here asks you not to manufacture the turn but to recognize it, and to let yourself believe a deliverance too large for your shrunken hope. The dawn arrives looking so improbable that the first faithful response is dazed, disbelieving gladness.
upheaval.inYou: When the reversal finally comes after the long wait, you may not trust it. You may move through it dazed, braced for it to vanish, unable to feel the joy you once pictured. That is not failure of faith; it is the honest jolt of a rescue bigger than your hope had room for. Let yourself be glad slowly. The dream, this time, is true.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can stay in exile so long it forgets exile has an end, until renewal feels naive and Babylon feels permanent. Psalm 126 is the body's memory against that forgetting: God brought a whole people home, and they were like those who dream. A community holding this hope keeps alive the sentence it will one day say dazed and laughing — the LORD has done great things for us.
upheaval.whatRemains: Babylon felt unshakable for seventy years, and it was removed. What endures is not any captivity, however long, but the LORD who ends exiles. What can be shaken — even a settled, decorated, lifelong captivity — is shaken loose so that the unshakable thing stands clear: a God who still does great things, and brings His people home.
reflection: Have I quietly stopped expecting my exile to end, and started decorating Babylon as if it were home?
If God brought the reversal I had given up naming, would I trust it, or brace for it to dissolve?
Can I say, even dazed and half-disbelieving, that the LORD has done great things for me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, my exile has gone on so long I had nearly stopped expecting it to end. Forgive me for making a home in Babylon and calling hope naive. Bring me back to Zion. And when You do, steady my dazed heart to say the true thing: the LORD has done great things for us. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 126:1, 3 (the return to Zion; we were like those who dream).
notes.tradition: References the return of the Judean exiles from Babylon beginning in 538 BC under the decree of Cyrus; general history, paraphrased.

title: The unlikely deliverer
moment: It is one of the most jarring sentences in the prophets. The LORD speaks of His anointed — the word is messiah, the title saved for kings of David's line and finally for Christ Himself — and the name He attaches to it is Cyrus. A Persian. A pagan emperor who worshipped other gods and had, until that decree, never given Israel's God a thought. God says He took this man by the right hand, the way one leads a chosen instrument, that He called him by name and gave him a title of honor. And then, lest anyone soften the scandal, He adds the line that makes the whole thing stranger still: though you have not known me. The deliverer who ends the seventy-year exile is not a returning prophet, not a hidden Israelite hero raised up in secret. He is an outsider who does not know the God using him, going about his own imperial business of subduing nations, unaware that his right hand is being held. The hinge of an entire people's rescue turns on a man who could not have named the One who chose him.
voiceQuote: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have held, to subdue nations before him.
scriptureText: For Jacob my servant's sake, I have called you by your name; I have surnamed you, though you have not known me.
weight: We have a quiet assumption that God's deliverance will come through approved channels — the faithful person, the sound source, the help that arrives already speaking our language and sharing our convictions. Cyrus breaks that assumption clean in half. The instrument God appoints to end the exile fails every test we would have set. He is foreign, he is pagan, and he does not know the LORD at all. And he is, nonetheless, the LORD's anointed for this work, because the Lord of history is not confined to the means His people find respectable. This does not collapse every distinction; it does not make every outsider a Cyrus or every secular force a deliverance. But it should permanently loosen our grip on the idea that God can only reach us through the doors we approve. Your rescue may arrive in a hand you would never have shaken, through a person who has no idea they are being used, by a means you had ruled out as unspiritual. Do not despise the unlikely instrument. The hand holding it may be the LORD's.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn through the most unexpected door — deliverance arriving by an instrument no one watching would have chosen. The phase asks you to widen your sense of how rescue can come, to stop scanning only the approved channels. The turn out of the wilderness often walks in wearing the wrong clothes, sent by a hand you did not see at work.
upheaval.inYou: Your deliverance may come through someone you would never have picked, or even approved — an outsider, a stranger, a person with no idea God is using them for your good. Cyrus did not know the LORD, and the LORD used him anyway. Do not wait only for help that already shares your language and convictions. God's hand reaches you through instruments you would not have chosen.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church watching for rescue only through familiar, sanctioned channels may miss the Cyrus God has already appointed — the unexpected ally, the secular instrument, the stranger who serves a purpose he cannot name. God has delivered His people through pagan kings before. A community too sure of which doors God uses can stand waiting at them while deliverance walks in through a door it had bolted.
upheaval.whatRemains: When God reaches you through a hand you would never have chosen, your idea of His acceptable means is shaken off. What is removed is the assumption that He is confined to the channels we approve. What remains is the Lord of all history, free to take any right hand He pleases, unconfined to the doors we leave open.
reflection: Am I watching for deliverance only through channels I already approve?
Is there an unlikely instrument in my situation I have despised because of who it came through?
Can I trust the Lord of history to use even someone who does not know Him, for my good?
upheaval.prayer: Lord of all history, I confess I have wanted rescue only through doors I find respectable, and despised the help that came otherwise. You called a pagan king Your anointed. Open my eyes to the Cyrus You have appointed for me, and let me receive Your deliverance through whatever hand You choose to hold. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 45:1, 4 (Cyrus, the LORD's anointed, called though he did not know God).
notes.tradition: References the Persian king Cyrus, whose decree (c. 539-538 BC) ended the Babylonian exile; general history, paraphrased.

title: The years restored
moment: The locust does not kill in an afternoon. It works in waves, swarm after swarm, the swarming and the hopping and the destroying and the cutting, until what was a green land is stubble and the years themselves seem eaten. Joel had watched it happen — a nation stripped bare, season after season devoured, the kind of slow ruin that makes you stop counting what you have lost because the losing will not stop. And then, to that emptied land, God makes a promise so large it almost overreaches grief itself. He does not say only that the plague will end, that next year the swarms will stay away. He says He will restore the years that the swarming locust has eaten. Not the fields — the years. The time itself. The seasons that were stripped clean and seemed simply gone, written off as waste, are named as recoverable. And the promise does not stop at restoration; it runs on to satisfaction. You will eat in plenty and be satisfied, Joel says, and praise the name of the LORD your God who has dealt wondrously. The God who lets nothing be wasted reaches back into the eaten years and gives them.
voiceQuote: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten.
scriptureText: You will have plenty to eat, and be satisfied, and will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has dealt wondrously with you.
weight: Of all the griefs the wilderness hands you, the grief of lost time may be the heaviest, because it seems the one thing past undoing. A broken thing can be mended, a wound can heal, but a year the locust ate is simply gone — you cannot live it again. So we make a quiet peace with the waste. We tell ourselves the years to illness or addiction, to depression or doubt or sheer aimless wandering, are a sunk cost, a write-off best not examined. Joel's promise dares more than that peace allows. It does not merely comfort you about the future; it makes a claim on the past. God can take the eaten years and redeem them — fold them into a story where even the waste turns out to have been doing something, where the lost time is given back fruitful. This is more than survival, more than starting over from where the swarms left off. It is the redemption of loss itself. The years you have written off are not beyond His restoring. He deals wondrously, and the wonder reaches backward.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn at its most daring — the turn promising not merely an end to the devouring but the restoration of what was devoured. The phase asks you to hope past survival, to believe God can redeem the very years the wilderness ate. The dawn here does not just stop the loss going forward; it reaches back into the eaten time and gives it.
upheaval.inYou: You may be grieving wasted years — time the locusts of illness, addiction, depression, or sheer wandering ate clean away, years you have quietly written off as gone. Joel's promise dares more than you would: God restores the years the locust has eaten. He can not only end the devouring but redeem the lost time, making even the wasted years bear fruit. They are not beyond His restoring.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church mourning wasted years — a lost generation, decades of decline, seasons the locust stripped bare — can scarcely picture them redeemed, and so makes peace with the waste. Joel refuses that peace on the body's behalf: God restores the years the locust has eaten. A community's wasted seasons are not past His power to redeem and make fruitful. Restoration, not mere survival, is the scope of the promise.
upheaval.whatRemains: When God reaches back into the eaten years, even the past stops being fixed and final. What is shaken loose is the verdict that the lost time is simply gone, beyond redeeming. What remains is the God who wastes nothing, whose restoring power is not bounded by the calendar, and who gives back fruitful even the years the locust ate.
reflection: What years have I quietly written off as wasted, beyond any redeeming?
Do I believe God's restoration reaches only forward, or back into the eaten time as well?
Can I hope past mere survival, to a God who deals wondrously even with my lost years?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have made a quiet peace with the years the locust ate, and called them simply gone. You promise more. Reach back into the wasted seasons and redeem them. Give back fruitful what I had written off, and let me praise You as the God who deals wondrously, even with lost time. Amen.

notes.primary: Joel 2:25-26 (I will restore the years the locust has eaten; you will be satisfied).

title: Watchman, what of the night?
moment: Out of the dark of Seir a voice calls up to the watchman on the wall, and the question is the oldest one the night knows: watchman, what of the night? It comes twice, the way real dread repeats itself — how much is left, is there any end to this, will the dark ever break. The watchman's answer in Isaiah is famously cryptic: the morning comes, and also the night. The dawn is real, he says, but more darkness may come too; he will not lie about the second half to comfort you with the first. It is the honest answer of someone who has actually stood the long watches. But the question does not stay in Isaiah. Paul takes it up and answers the church far more boldly. The night, he says, is far gone, and the day is near. So far gone, in fact, that you can already start to dress for daylight — throw off the works of darkness, the things that belong only to the night, and put on the armor of light. The watcher who knows morning is coming does not merely endure the last hours. He begins, in the dark, to get ready for the day.
voiceQuote: One calls to me out of Seir, Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?
scriptureText: The night is far gone, and the day is near; therefore let us throw off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light.
weight: There is a way of waiting that is purely passive — hunched against the cold, counting the hours, doing nothing but surviving until the dark relents. And there is another way, the way Paul presses on a church still in the night. If the day is truly near, the dark hours change character. They stop being a sentence to be served and become a threshold to be dressed for. You can begin to live now as one who knows morning is coming — laying aside the deeds that only made sense in the darkness, the habits and despairs that assumed the night was permanent, and putting on instead the conduct of the daylight that is on its way. This is not pretending the night is over; the watchman is honest that it is not, that more dark may yet come. It is living by the certainty of the dawn before you can see it. The weary watcher who believes morning is coming keeps watch differently from one who fears it never will — and that difference, the dressing for a day not yet visible, is itself part of the turn.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation turning toward dawn made personal as a question and an answer — how much night remains, and the word that morning is coming. The phase asks you to keep watch differently, to live now by the certainty of a dawn you cannot yet see. The turn is partly this: dressing for the day while it is still dark, because the night is far gone.
upheaval.inYou: You have asked the watchman's question in your own dark — how much longer, is there any end. The answer of faith is that morning comes; the night is far gone and the day is near. You can begin, even now, to live as one expecting dawn: throwing off the works of darkness, dressing for daylight on its way. The watcher who knows morning is coming keeps watch differently.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church in a long night cries the watchman's question too: how much longer. The answer is that the night is far gone and the day is near. A community can begin to live toward the dawn before it breaks — laying aside the works of darkness, putting on the armor of light, carrying itself as a people who know morning comes. Expectant living is itself part of the turn.
upheaval.whatRemains: The night feels permanent while you stand in it, but night is the one thing that cannot last; it is shaken off by the morning. What is removed is the darkness and the deeds that belonged to it. What remains is the day that is near and the God who brings it — the dawn no night can hold back.
reflection: What is the works of darkness I am still wearing, as if the night were permanent?
Am I waiting for dawn passively, or beginning even now to dress for the day?
Can I keep watch as one who knows morning is coming, even before I can see it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have cried the watchman's question in my own dark — how much longer. You answer that the night is far gone and the day is near. Help me believe it before I see it, throw off the works of darkness, and keep watch as one who knows morning is coming. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 21:11 (watchman, what of the night?); Romans 13:12 (the night is far gone, the day is near).

title: That I may see again
moment: Bartimaeus sits where the blind always sit, at the edge of the road, begging. He cannot see Jesus coming, but he hears the crowd change, and that is enough. He starts to shout, and when they tell him to hush he only shouts louder, because a blind man learns that his voice is the one thing he still owns. Jesus stops. Call him. And the question Jesus asks is almost startling in its openness: what do you want me to do for you? A blind beggar could ask for many things — money, safety, a better corner. What he asks for is the thing underneath all the others. Rabboni, that I may see again. Notice the again. He had not always been blind; there was a time he could see, and the darkness came later and took it. He is not asking for something new so much as the return of something lost. And when the sight comes back, he does not gather his cloak and go home to the old corner. He follows Jesus down the road. Recovered sight, the moment it is given, becomes a direction.
voiceQuote: Rabboni, that I may see again.
scriptureText: Your faith has made you well. Immediately he received his sight, and followed Jesus in the way.
weight: Most of the long wilderness is a slow going-blind. Not all at once, but by degrees: the sense of God dims, the way forward greys over, the meaning of things you once saw plainly fogs and then is gone. You learn to beg at the edge of the road because you cannot find the road. And the temptation, when help finally comes near, is to ask for the wrong thing — to ask for the corner improved rather than the eyes opened, for circumstances rearranged rather than sight restored. Bartimaeus asks for the deeper thing, and it is the prayer that turns disorientation toward its dawn. Not first a changed life, but the ability to see again — to see God, to see the way, to see that any of it means something after all. And the proof that the sight is real is where it sends you. He did not blink in the new light and shuffle back to the familiar dark. He fell in behind Jesus on the road. Sight that does not lead to following was never the sight worth asking for.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the turn within disorientation, where the long blindness begins to lift. The wilderness is, in large part, a loss of sight — of God, of the way, of the point. The phase asks you to name that honestly and to make the beggar's bold cry: not for the corner improved, but for the eyes opened, that you might see again and follow.
upheaval.inYou: Look at what the wilderness has dimmed in you — your sense of God, your read of the way, your hold on what any of it means. The thing to beg for is not a better corner but new sight. Make Bartimaeus's prayer your own: Lord, that I may see again. And when the seeing returns, let it lead you not back to the old dark but forward, behind Him.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church climbing out of disorientation needs, before any program, to see again — to recover the vision of God the wilderness dimmed and the sense of the way it lost. The body that begs only for its corner improved misses the deeper gift. Ask, like Bartimaeus, for opened eyes, and let restored sight send the community down the road after Christ, not back to the old ways.
upheaval.whatRemains: Sight can be lost and given back, but the One who restores it does not change. When the wilderness has shaken away every clear thing you thought you saw, what cannot be shaken is the Lord who stops on the road for a blind man's cry and opens his eyes. The Giver remains when the darkness is removed.
reflection: What has my wilderness made me blind to that I once saw plainly?
Am I begging for my corner improved, or for the deeper gift of sight?
If my eyes were opened today, would I follow Him down the road or shuffle back to the old dark?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the long wilderness has dimmed my sight until I can no longer see You or the way. I will not be quiet about it. Rabboni, that I may see again. Open my eyes, and when they open, set my feet behind You on the road. Amen.

notes.primary: Mark 10:51-52 (Bartimaeus asks to see again, and follows Jesus).

title: The plowman overtakes the reaper
moment: Amos has been a hard book to read. Page after page of thunder, the plumb line held against a crooked nation, the warnings that the day of the LORD would be darkness and not light. And then, at the very end, the storm breaks open into something almost too lavish to picture. The days come, says the LORD, when the plowman shall overtake the reaper. Stop and see it: the harvest is so enormous that the man gathering this year's grain is still working when the man breaking ground for next year's catches up to him, the seasons of plenty crowding into each other with no lean gap between. The mountains drop sweet wine. The waste cities, the ones reduced to rubble in the judgment, are rebuilt and lived in. Vineyards are planted by the very people who will drink from them. After all that thunder, the last word out of Amos is not survival but overflow — abundance so generous it cannot keep up with itself, breaking out on the far side of the wilderness like a harvest that refuses to end.
voiceQuote: The days come, says the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the mountains shall drop sweet wine.
scriptureText: I will bring back the captivity of my people; they shall build the waste cities, and inhabit them, and plant vineyards.
weight: Long scarcity does something quiet and corrosive to the imagination. When the wilderness has been lean for years, you stop being able to picture abundance; you learn to ask only for enough, and even that feels presumptuous. Hope shrinks to fit the famine. Amos will not let it stay shrunk. The God who held the plumb line is the same God promising the plowman who overtakes the reaper, and He means it as more than relief. He means overflow — a fullness so excessive the harvest spills into the next planting. This matters because the turn out of disorientation tempts you to settle for bare recovery, to be grateful merely to have survived and ask nothing further. But the promise on the table is larger. God is not a stingy restorer who returns you to zero and calls it kindness. The waste cities are not merely cleared; they are inhabited. The vineyards are not merely planted; they are enjoyed. Do not let the lean years be the measure of what you expect from His abundance.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the turn within disorientation, lifting the eyes past mere survival toward overflow. The wilderness teaches you to expect scarcity and to call recovery enough. The phase asks you to let God enlarge the imagination the famine shrank — to believe the restoration ahead is not a grudging return to zero but an abundance that outpaces itself.
upheaval.inYou: The wilderness has been lean so long you may have quietly stopped expecting more than survival. Amos dares you wider: days are coming when the harvest overtakes the planting, when there is more than enough. Do not let the famine set the ceiling on God's generosity. His restoration is no careful return to zero; it is overflow, the seasons of plenty running into each other.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church formed by long scarcity can lose the very capacity to imagine abundance, learning to be grateful merely to have endured. Amos's vision is unembarrassed by largeness: the plowman overtaking the reaper, waste cities rebuilt, vineyards planted and enjoyed. The body's restoration is not grudging recovery but overflow. After the lean years, a community may lift its eyes to a generosity that outruns itself.
upheaval.whatRemains: Harvests come and fail; lean years strip the imagination bare. But the God who promises the plowman overtaking the reaper does not run dry with the land. When scarcity has shaken away your expectation of anything beyond survival, what cannot be shaken is the lavish generosity of the One whose restoration is overflow.
reflection: Has long scarcity quietly shrunk what I dare to expect from God?
Am I asking only to survive when He is offering overflow?
Where might I be calling bare recovery enough, and missing the abundance He intends?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the lean years have taught me to expect little and to call survival a kindness. Enlarge what I dare to hope for. You promise the plowman overtaking the reaper, the waste places rebuilt and lived in. Lift my eyes past mere recovery to Your overflow. Amen.

notes.primary: Amos 9:13-14 (the plowman overtakes the reaper; the waste cities rebuilt).

title: The bones stand up
moment: Once, in the deep of the wilderness, God set Ezekiel in a valley of dry bones and asked the cruel-seeming question: can these bones live? And Ezekiel, who could not say yes to the evidence and dared not say no to the LORD, handed it back: Lord, you know. This is the day the answer comes. God tells him to prophesy, and as the words leave his mouth there is a sound, a rattling, and across the whole valley bone finds bone. Sinew threads them, flesh climbs over them, skin draws shut. And yet they are not alive; they lie there, whole and still, bodies without breath, which is somehow worse than scattered bone. So God sends the prophet to call the breath itself from the four winds, and the breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, an exceedingly great army. Look at the distance covered. From very many and very dry to a host standing upright and breathing. The deadest valley the prophet could be shown does not get tidied or improved. It is raised. God did not answer the question with an argument. He answered it with resurrection.
voiceQuote: The breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
scriptureText: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land.
weight: There was a day you stood over your own valley and could not lie about the bones. The dried-up calling, the relationship gone to powder, the faith you feared was finished — you looked honestly, refused the hollow yes, and handed the verdict back: Lord, you know. This is the payoff of that honesty. The God to whom you handed the impossible question is the God who breathes on dust until it stands. He does not specialize in improving dying things; He specializes in raising dead ones. Optimism says the bones were not really so dry; faith admits they were bone, and waits for the breath anyway. The breath came. It always was His to send and never yours to manufacture, and that is precisely why it could come at all — resurrection is the craft of God, not the achievement of the determined. What you gave up for dead was not beyond Him. The honest no you refused to speak was the right restraint, because He had a yes you could not have seen.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the turn at its most dramatic, disorientation answered by resurrection. The valley where everything looked dead is not merely eased; it is raised. The phase asks you to let the breath come where you had only learned to grieve, and to receive as God's gift the life you could neither produce nor, as it turns out, rule out.
upheaval.inYou: The dry bones you once handed back to God with Lord, you know — this is His answer over them. The deadest thing in you is not beyond resurrection. He does not merely tidy dying situations; He breathes His Spirit into bone-dry dust until what you buried stands up alive. You were right not to force a yes and not to rule out a no. The breath can still come.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that surveyed itself and saw only a valley of bones — life gone, hope desiccated, nothing left but skeleton — is exactly the ground God loves to raise. The answer to can these bones live is the rattling, the standing, the exceedingly great army on its feet. The Spirit who raised a slaughtered valley can do the same to a church counted gone.
upheaval.whatRemains: Everything that can dry up does; hope itself goes to powder, and the valley fills with bone. But the breath of God is not subject to the death it stands over. When all that can die has died and been shaken away, what cannot be shaken is the living Spirit who raises what no will of yours could revive.
reflection: What did I once hand back to God as too dead to live, saying only Lord, you know?
Do I still believe He raises dead things, or have I quietly settled for improving them?
Where am I waiting for a breath only He can send, and refusing to call it finished?
upheaval.prayer: Lord GOD, once I stood over dry bones and could only say that You knew. Here is Your answer: You breathe, and the dead stand up. Send Your breath into what I gave up for lost. Raise what I could never revive, until it stands on its feet alive. Amen.

notes.primary: Ezekiel 37:10, 14 (the breath enters the bones; they live and stand; I will put my Spirit in you).

title: Carrying the sheaves
moment: The pilgrims' psalm, having marveled that the return from exile felt like a dream, turns at the end to make a plainer promise, the kind you can lean your weight on. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will assuredly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves. Picture the sower it describes. He is not striding out in confidence; he is weeping as he goes, scattering precious grain into hard ground he is not sure will yield, grain he could have eaten, given to the dirt instead. It looks like loss. It looks like a grieving man throwing away what little he has. But the psalm names it for what it is: not waste, but sowing. The tears do not cancel the seed; they water it. And the promise attached is not a maybe — it is assuredly. He will come again, and the going-out and the coming-back are set against each other deliberately: out with weeping and seed, back with joy and sheaves. James adds the one thing the psalm leaves implied, the virtue that fills the gap between sowing and harvest. The farmer waits for the precious fruit, patient over it, through the early rains and the late.
voiceQuote: He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will assuredly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
scriptureText: Be patient, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. The farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it.
weight: The hardest thing to believe in the wilderness is that the costly, fruitless-looking faithfulness counts for anything. The prayers that seemed to fall on dry ground. The obedience no one saw and nothing rewarded. The quiet sowing of yourself into a season that gave nothing visible back. It felt like throwing away what little you had — like the weeping sower scattering his bread on the dirt. The psalm insists it was seed. Not wasted, not leaked away pointlessly, but planted, and there is a harvest coming from it as surely as anything in this life is sure. What the promise does not do is name the date, and that omission is where James does his quiet work. Between the sowing and the reaping lies the long patience of the farmer, who cannot hurry the grain and cannot skip the rains. The turn does not arrive on your schedule. But it arrives. The one who went out weeping does come back carrying sheaves. Your tears in the wilderness were not the end of the story; they were planting something you will one day gather with joy.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the turn within disorientation, where the seed sown in tears begins, at last, to come up as harvest. The phase asks you to trust two things at once: that the costly faithfulness of the wilderness was sowing and not waste, and that the reaping, though it comes on God's timetable and not yours, comes assuredly — and to keep the farmer's patience until it does.
upheaval.inYou: Everything you sowed in tears through the wilderness — the unseen faithfulness, the prayers that seemed to land on stone, the obedience that cost you and paid nothing back — was seed, not waste. The promise is sure: you will come again carrying sheaves. It asks the farmer's patience, the long wait through the rains. But the weeping sower does become the rejoicing reaper.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church that sowed in tears through its wilderness — faithful labor with no visible fruit, costly obedience held through lean years — is promised a reaping. The seed was not lost in the weeping; it was planted. With the farmer's patience, through the early and the late rains, the community that went out weeping comes back carrying sheaves. The harvest is sure, though its timing is not the body's.
upheaval.whatRemains: Timetables are not ours, and the long wait can shake your confidence that the sowing meant anything. But the faithfulness of the God who keeps the promise does not waver with the seasons. When patience has worn away every other assurance, what cannot be shaken is His sure word: the weeping sower will assuredly come again carrying the sheaves.
reflection: What have I sown in tears that I quietly fear was simply wasted?
Do I believe the harvest is sure, even though its timing is not mine to set?
Where do I need the farmer's patience, waiting through the rains for fruit I cannot yet see?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have sown so much in tears and seen no harvest, and I fear it was all for nothing. Teach me it was seed, not waste. Give me the farmer's patience through the long rains, and bring me back at last with joy, carrying the sheaves. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 126:6 (weeping sower returns with sheaves); James 5:7 (the farmer's patience for the fruit).

title: Tomorrow the LORD will do wonders
figure: At the edge of the Jordan
moment: Forty years of wandering come down to a riverbank. The wilderness generation has died in the sand; a new one stands at the Jordan with the promised land lying green across the water, close enough to see and not yet theirs to walk. It is a strange, charged place to stand — the old wandering finished, the new country in plain sight, and a river still between. And Joshua's word to the people on that threshold is not a battle plan. It is not even a map. It is this: sanctify yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you. Make yourselves ready, set yourselves apart, because the God who walked you all the way through the wilderness is about to act, and the acting is His. The promise behind it had already been spoken: every place the sole of your foot shall tread, I have given you. The land is gift before it is conquest. So they stand at the edge of everything they have waited for, told not to strategize but to consecrate, because the crossing belongs to the LORD, and tomorrow He will do wonders. The wilderness has delivered them, at last, here — to the brink of the new.
voiceQuote: Sanctify yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.
scriptureText: Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread on, I have given you, as I spoke to Moses.
weight: This is where the long disorientation finally brings you: not back to the place you left, and not yet into the place you are going, but to the riverbank between — the wandering behind you, the new land in sight, a crossing still ahead. Thresholds have their own particular ache, because you can see the thing you longed for and cannot yet stand in it. The word for this place is not anxiety and not striving. It is consecration. Sanctify yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders. The work of the threshold is to ready your heart, not to force the river. And notice where the wonders are. They are not behind you, in the wilderness you survived; that was the wandering, not the wonder. The wonders are ahead, across the water, in the land God has already given before a single foot has touched it. Tomorrow is the word that matters. The God who proved faithful through every year of the wandering is not finished. The best of His faithfulness is on the far bank, and the wilderness has carried you all the way to its edge.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disorientation closing toward its threshold, the wilderness ending at the riverbank and the new land in view. The phase has done its long work and now hands you forward. It asks not for strategy but for consecration — to ready your heart at the brink, because the crossing belongs to the LORD, and tomorrow He will do wonders in the country He has already given.
upheaval.inYou: The wilderness brings you, at last, to a riverbank: the old wandering behind, the new land in sight but not yet entered. Hear Joshua's word for the threshold. Sanctify yourself, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders. The work here is not to force the crossing but to ready your heart. The wonders are not behind you in the wilderness you survived; they wait ahead.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church at the end of its wilderness stands where Israel stood: the wandering finished, the new country in view, the river still ahead. The word for that moment is not a strategy session but a consecration. Ready yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will act among you. A body that consecrates its heart at the riverbank is preparing to cross into the new bearings God is about to give.
upheaval.whatRemains: Thresholds give way; even the riverbank is a place you do not stay. But the faithfulness that walked you through the wandering does not stop at the water's edge. When the wilderness has shaken away all the rest, what cannot be shaken is the LORD who brought you here and goes on ahead: tomorrow He will do wonders.
reflection: Where has my wilderness brought me to a threshold I can see across but not yet enter?
Am I trying to force the crossing, or readying my heart as Joshua told the people to?
Do I expect the wonders behind me in what I survived, or ahead, in the land He has already given?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the long wandering has carried me to the riverbank, the new land in sight and the water still between. I will not force the crossing. I sanctify my heart and wait, for tomorrow You will do wonders. Lead me across into the country You have already given. Amen.

notes.primary: Joshua 3:5 (sanctify yourselves, tomorrow the LORD will do wonders); Joshua 1:3 (every place your foot treads I have given you).
